subject: VAPA
overview: Plan about 30 minutes a day. Units alternate between visual art studios (drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture) and music (rhythm, recorder, singing, listening, composing), with art and songs tied to fifth-grade early-American history. You don't need to be an artist or musician: show the reference image or recording, demonstrate the technique roughly, and let your child practice; judge growth against the stated cues and rubrics, not 'talent.' Keep a sketchbook and a portfolio folder all year, use the four critique steps (describe, analyze, interpret, judge), and record music performances so your child can self-evaluate.

weeks.prep: Gather a sketchbook, pencils, a fine-tip marker, and a few objects with interesting edges (a shoe, a houseplant, a kitchen whisk). Set a timer for gesture drawings. Contour = a line drawing of edges; blind contour = drawing while looking only at the object.
misconceptions: Thinking blind contour drawings should look 'right.' They are meant to look wobbly — the goal is training the eye to look closely, not a realistic picture.
Drawing slowly and stiffly in gesture drawing. Gesture is fast, loose and about the action/movement, not details.

days.guide: Show examples of line types and talk about moods (zigzag = energetic or tense, wavy = calm, broken = uncertain). Your child fills a page with 12 labeled line types.

questions.q: What mood might a thick, jagged zigzag line suggest? A thin, wavy line?
questions.a: Zigzag: excitement, anger, danger or energy. Wavy: calm, gentle, flowing movement.

days.guide: Your child places their non-drawing hand in a pose and draws it three times without looking at the paper, moving the pen slowly as the eyes trace each edge.

questions.q: Why draw without looking at the paper?
questions.a: It forces you to look carefully at the object's edges and connects the eye and hand, improving observation.

days.guide: Draw a shoe or plant with modified contour: mostly look at the object, glance at the paper only to place the pen at a new edge.

questions.q: How is modified contour different from blind contour?
questions.a: In modified contour you can glance at the paper occasionally to check placement; in blind contour you never look.

days.guide: Have a family member strike action poses for 30 seconds each; your child draws the whole body quickly with flowing lines, starting with the line of action (spine).

questions.q: What is the goal of a gesture drawing?
questions.a: To capture the movement and overall pose quickly, not the details.

days.guide: Your child picks the best contour drawing and writes two sentences with art vocabulary (line weight, contour, continuous, varied).

questions.q: What is line quality?
questions.a: The character of a line — thick/thin, light/dark, smooth/rough — that gives a drawing expression.

weeks.assessment_key: Sketchbook check: line sampler with 12 labeled lines and moods; 3 blind contours; 1 modified contour; 10 gestures. Reflection rubric: 4 = two sentences using at least two art terms (contour, line weight, gesture) accurately about a specific drawing; 3 = one term; 2 = general description; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather HB, 2B and 4B pencils (B pencils are softer and darker), a blending stump or tissue, an egg or ball, and a flashlight. Find a Leonardo da Vinci drawing on Google Arts & Culture (e.g., a drapery study or 'Head of a Woman').
misconceptions: Outlining shaded objects with a dark line. Real objects show edges through changes in value, not outlines.
Forgetting the cast shadow or attaching it wrongly. The cast shadow falls on the surface on the side opposite the light.

days.guide: Draw a 7-box strip; shade from white to darkest by pressure. Make a second strip using hatching (parallel lines) and cross-hatching (crossed lines) — closer lines are darker.

questions.q: How do you make a darker value with hatching?
questions.a: Draw lines closer together, add more layers of crossed lines (cross-hatching), or press harder.

days.guide: Demonstrate one light source; your child shades a sphere, cube and cylinder with highlight, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow.

questions.q: If the light comes from the upper left, where will the cast shadow fall?
questions.a: On the surface to the lower right of the object.

days.guide: Darken the room, shine a flashlight on an egg, and draw it, matching values to the value scale.

questions.q: What is a highlight?
questions.a: The brightest spot on an object, where light hits it most directly.

days.guide: Look at a Leonardo drawing; your child points to areas of hatching and soft blending. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How did Leonardo show form in his drawings?
questions.a: With careful value changes — hatching lines (often diagonal, since he was left-handed) and soft gradual shading to make forms look round.

days.guide: Your child draws a 2-object still life and checks: full range of values, highlight, core shadow, cast shadow, consistent light direction.

questions.q: Why must all shadows go the same direction?
questions.a: There's one light source, so all shadows fall consistently away from it; otherwise the drawing looks unrealistic.

weeks.assessment_key: Value scales: 7 even steps from white to near black (pressure) and with hatching/cross-hatching. Still life checklist: (1) one consistent light source (2) highlight (3) core shadow (4) cast shadow (5) at least 5 distinct values. 4 = all five; 3 = four; 2 = two or three; 1 = one or none.

weeks.prep: Gather a ruler, pencil, eraser and sketchbook. Practice one-point perspective yourself once first: a horizontal horizon line, one dot (vanishing point) on it, and lines from box corners to that dot.
misconceptions: Placing the vanishing point off the horizon line. In one-point perspective, the vanishing point always sits on the horizon line.
Drawing all receding lines to different points. All lines going 'into' the picture meet at the single vanishing point; vertical lines stay vertical and horizontal lines stay horizontal.

days.guide: Your child draws a landscape using overlapping, size change (far = smaller) and placement (far = higher on the page) to show foreground, middle ground and background.

questions.q: Name three ways to show depth without perspective lines.
questions.a: Overlapping, size (farther objects smaller), and placement (farther objects higher on the page); also less detail and lighter color in the distance.

days.guide: Draw a horizon line and vanishing point. Your child draws squares above, below and on the line, connects corners to the vanishing point, and closes the boxes.

questions.q: If you draw a box below the horizon line, which side can you see?
questions.a: The top of the box.

days.guide: Draw a road or hallway narrowing to the vanishing point; add trees or doors that get smaller as they go back.

questions.q: Why do trees along the road get smaller toward the vanishing point?
questions.a: Objects appear smaller the farther they are from the viewer.

days.guide: Your child begins a perspective drawing of a meaningful place (street, room, favorite spot), placing the horizon at eye level.

questions.q: Where should the horizon line be in your drawing?
questions.a: At your eye level.

days.guide: Finish the drawing; label the horizon line and vanishing point. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is a vanishing point?
questions.a: The point on the horizon line where parallel lines going away from the viewer appear to meet.

weeks.assessment_key: Perspective drawing rubric: 4 = horizon line and vanishing point labeled, all receding lines converge correctly, objects shrink with distance, foreground/middle/background clear, place meaningful; 3 = minor line errors; 2 = inconsistent perspective; 1 = no perspective.

weeks.prep: Cut a cardboard viewfinder (a 2 × 3 inch window in cardstock). Gather drawing paper and pencils. Learn the 'I notice, I wonder' feedback format.
misconceptions: Thinking the first drawing should be the final. Thumbnails let you try compositions quickly before committing.
Giving every area equal detail. A focal point is where the most contrast and detail go, guiding the viewer's eye.

days.guide: Your child uses the viewfinder to frame three views of a corner of the home and makes a quick thumbnail of each, then picks one.

questions.q: What is a composition?
questions.a: The arrangement of the parts of an artwork.

days.guide: Lightly block in the chosen view with contour lines and perspective, keeping lines light for changes.

questions.q: Why draw lightly at first?
questions.a: So you can erase and change without leaving marks.

days.guide: Add value and texture; make the focal point have the strongest contrast and most detail. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How can you make a focal point stand out?
questions.a: Use the strongest contrast, most detail, or place it where lines lead the eye.

days.guide: Give 'I notice, I wonder' feedback; your child makes one revision. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Give an example of 'I notice, I wonder' feedback.
questions.a: 'I notice the chair has strong shadows. I wonder if the background could be lighter to make the chair stand out.'

days.guide: Your child writes an artist statement (what, how, why, revision) and files the drawing. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What belongs in an artist statement?
questions.a: What the artwork shows, techniques and choices made, the focal point and why, and what was revised.

weeks.assessment_key: Drawing rubric (1–4 each): composition (thumbnail-based, clear focal point); accurate contour and perspective; full value range and texture; craftsmanship; revision shown. Artist statement: proficient names subject, two techniques, focal point choice and the revision made.

weeks.prep: Bookmark musictheory.net (Lessons: Note Duration, Measures and Time Signature) and gather 8 rhythm cards (quarter notes, eighth pairs, half notes, whole notes, quarter rests). Choose three recordings: a march (e.g., Sousa 'Stars and Stripes Forever'), a waltz (e.g., Strauss 'Blue Danube'), and a pop song in 4.
misconceptions: Confusing the beat with the rhythm. The beat is the steady pulse; the rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds over it.
Thinking a rest means stop counting. Rests take up beats of silence; keep counting through them.

days.guide: Play each recording; your child pats the beat and finds the strong beat (beat 1) to decide if it's in 2, 3 or 4.

questions.q: A waltz feels 'ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three.' What meter is it in?
questions.a: Triple meter (3/4).

days.guide: Do the musictheory.net note-duration lessons; clap and count 8 rhythm cards ('1-and-2-and').

questions.q: How many beats does a half note get in 4/4? A whole note?
questions.a: Half note = 2 beats; whole note = 4 beats.

days.guide: Your child draws bar lines in 6 rhythm lines (2/4, 3/4, 4/4), counting beats per measure. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What does the top number of a time signature tell you?
questions.a: How many beats are in each measure (the bottom number tells which note gets one beat; 4 = quarter note).

days.guide: Clap 6 short rhythms; your child writes each in notation. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Write the rhythm for 'ta ta ti-ti ta.'
questions.a: Quarter, quarter, two eighth notes, quarter (4 beats).

days.guide: Your child sight-claps a 4-measure rhythm and takes the note-value quiz. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: How many eighth notes equal one quarter note?
questions.a: Two.

weeks.assessment_key: Note-value quiz: whole = 4 beats; half = 2; quarter = 1; eighth = ½; quarter rest = 1; half rest = 2; whole rest = 4 (or a full measure); two eighths = 1 beat; 3/4 = 3 beats per measure. Sight-clapping: 4 = steady beat, all rhythms correct; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors or unsteady beat; 1 = cannot complete.

weeks.prep: Open Chrome Music Lab Rhythm. Gather buckets or pots and wooden spoons. Find recordings of 'America the Beautiful' and Scott Joplin's 'The Entertainer' or 'Maple Leaf Rag.'
misconceptions: Thinking a dot adds one beat. A dot adds half of the note's value (dotted half = 3 beats; dotted quarter = 1½ beats).
Rushing improvised solos. An improvised solo must still fit the steady beat and the length (4 measures).

days.guide: Teach dotted half (3 beats) and dotted quarter (1½ beats, usually followed by an eighth). Clap 'O beau-ti-ful for spa-cious skies' noticing the long-short pattern.

questions.q: How many beats is a dotted half note? A dotted quarter?
questions.a: Dotted half = 3 beats; dotted quarter = 1½ beats.

days.guide: Clap syncopated patterns (ti-ta-ti: eighth-quarter-eighth); listen for off-beat accents in Joplin's rag.

questions.q: What is syncopation?
questions.a: Accenting a weak beat or off-beat instead of the strong beat, which gives music a 'bouncy' feel.

days.guide: Your child creates a 4-beat body percussion ostinato (e.g., stomp-pat-clap-snap) and performs it with a recording.

questions.q: What is an ostinato?
questions.a: A short pattern repeated over and over.

days.guide: Take turns: you play 4 measures, your child answers with an improvised 4 measures on a bucket.

questions.q: What is improvisation?
questions.a: Making up music on the spot.

days.guide: Your child performs the ostinato and an improvised solo; evaluate with a steady-beat rubric.

questions.q: Why is a steady beat important in a performance with others?
questions.a: It keeps everyone together in time.

weeks.assessment_key: Steady-beat rubric: 4 = ostinato repeats correctly at least 8 times on beat, solo is exactly 4 measures with a steady beat and varied rhythms; 3 = minor slips; 2 = beat drifts often; 1 = no steady beat.

weeks.prep: Get a soprano recorder (baroque or German fingering — check which, since a few notes differ) and its fingering chart, or a free virtual recorder/keyboard app. Print flashcards of B, A and G on the treble staff and the music for 'Hot Cross Buns' (B A G, B A G, G G G G A A A A, B A G) and 'Gently Sleep.' Fingerings: B = left thumb + finger 1; A = thumb + 1, 2; G = thumb + 1, 2, 3.
misconceptions: Blowing too hard, which makes squeaks. Use gentle 'warm' breath, as if blowing on soup to cool it.
Leaky fingers. Cover holes with the pads of the fingers (not tips) so no air escapes; squeaks often mean a hole isn't fully covered.

days.guide: Show posture (sit or stand tall), left hand on top, lips gently around the mouthpiece (not teeth). Start each note with a soft 'too.' Play B (thumb + finger 1) with a steady tone.

questions.q: Which hand goes on top of the recorder?
questions.a: The left hand.

days.guide: Teach A (thumb + 1, 2) and G (thumb + 1, 2, 3). Play 4-note patterns: B-A-G-A, G-A-B-B. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What changes when you go from B to G?
questions.a: You cover more holes (add fingers 2 and 3), and the pitch gets lower.

days.guide: Flashcards: B on the middle line, A in the second space, G on the second line. Then play 'Hot Cross Buns' and 'Gently Sleep.'

questions.q: Which line of the treble staff is B on?
questions.a: The middle (third) line.

days.guide: Practice 10 minutes, then record 'Hot Cross Buns.' Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Why record yourself?
questions.a: So you can hear your tone and rhythm the way an audience does and find what to fix.

days.guide: Listen back and rate tone (no squeaks, steady) and rhythm (steady beat); then perform a B-A-G song for an audience.

questions.q: Your recording has squeaks. What two things should you check?
questions.a: Breath (blow more gently) and whether fingers fully cover the holes.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded performance rubric: 4 = correct notes, steady beat, clear tone with no squeaks, tonguing each note; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors or uneven rhythm; 1 = cannot complete. Self-evaluation proficient if it names one strength and one specific fix that matches the recording.

weeks.prep: Recorder, fingering chart and a metronome app. Print 'Merrily We Roll Along,' a simplified 'Ode to Joy' (B B C D D C B A G G A B B A A) and a 5-note warm-up. Fingerings (baroque and German are the same here): high C = thumb + finger 2; high D = finger 2 only (no thumb); low E = thumb + 1, 2, 3 (left) + 1, 2 (right hand).
misconceptions: Forgetting to lift the thumb for high D. High D uses only finger 2 of the left hand.
Playing louder to reach low notes. Low notes need gentler, slower breath.

days.guide: Teach high C (thumb + 2) and high D (2 only). Play 'Merrily We Roll Along' and sections of 'Old MacDonald.'

questions.q: What is the fingering for high D?
questions.a: Only the second finger of the left hand; no thumb.

days.guide: Teach low E using the right hand; play a 5-note warm-up (E-G-A-B-C or G-A-B-C-D) with a metronome at 60.

questions.q: Why use a metronome?
questions.a: To keep a steady tempo and notice rushing or slowing.

days.guide: Play 'Ode to Joy' with a sibling, parent or recording; start together after a count-off. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is an ensemble?
questions.a: A group of musicians performing together.

days.guide: Your child keeps a practice log: what they practiced, a tricky measure, and how they fixed it (slow practice, repeat 5 times).

questions.q: What's a good strategy for a tricky measure?
questions.a: Practice it slowly, alone, several times, then put it back in the song at tempo.

days.guide: Perform two recorder songs and a rhythm reading for family; evaluate with the rubric. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is a musical phrase?
questions.a: A musical 'sentence' — a group of notes that forms a complete idea, often ending at a breath.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (1–4 each): correct notes; steady rhythm; clear tone; phrasing/breathing at phrase ends; stage presence. Rhythm reading: correct counting of 4 measures. Proficient = 3+ in each category.

weeks.prep: Gather tempera or watercolors in red, yellow, blue, white and black; brushes, water cups, a palette (or paper plate) and paper. Draw a 12-section circle for the color wheel.
misconceptions: Thinking black and white are on the color wheel. They change value (tints and shades) but aren't hues on the wheel.
Muddy colors from dirty brushes. Rinse and blot between colors.

days.guide: Your child paints primaries (red, yellow, blue), mixes secondaries (orange, green, violet) between them, then tertiaries (red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet).

questions.q: How do you make a tertiary color?
questions.a: Mix a primary with the secondary next to it (e.g., blue + green = blue-green).

days.guide: Make a tint strip (add white in steps) and a shade strip (add black in small amounts) for one color.

questions.q: What's the difference between a tint and a shade?
questions.a: A tint adds white (lighter); a shade adds black (darker).

days.guide: Paint the same design with complementary (opposites), analogous (neighbors) and monochromatic (one hue with tints/shades) schemes.

questions.q: Name the complement of blue.
questions.a: Orange.

days.guide: Teach brush care (rinse, blot, reshape, store bristles up) and palette cleanup; compare moods of the three schemes.

questions.q: Which scheme usually feels calm and harmonious?
questions.a: Analogous (and monochromatic); complementary feels high-contrast and energetic.

days.guide: Take the quiz; your child writes which scheme they prefer and why. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: What are the three complementary pairs of primary/secondary colors?
questions.a: Red–green, blue–orange, yellow–violet (purple).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: primaries = red, yellow, blue; secondaries = orange, green, violet; tertiary = primary + adjacent secondary; complementary = opposite on wheel (red-green, blue-orange, yellow-violet); analogous = 3 neighbors; tint = + white; shade = + black; monochromatic = one hue. Color wheel rubric: 4 = all 12 colors mixed accurately in order; 3 = 1–2 off; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Open Thomas Cole's 'The Oxbow' (1836, Metropolitan Museum) and Albert Bierstadt's 'Looking Down Yosemite Valley' or 'Valley of the Yosemite' on Google Arts & Culture, plus a photo of Yosemite Valley. Find a Native American design or a modern landscape for comparison.
misconceptions: Thinking landscapes are exact copies of nature. Hudson River School painters often exaggerated light, scale and drama to stir emotion and celebrate American wilderness.
Thinking distant mountains should be painted darkest. Atmospheric perspective makes distant things lighter, bluer and less detailed.

days.guide: Your child studies 'The Oxbow' for 5 minutes and lists see/think/wonder. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What contrast does Cole show between the left and right sides of 'The Oxbow'?
questions.a: The left is wild, stormy wilderness; the right is sunny, calm, cultivated farmland along the river.

days.guide: Point out lighter, bluer distant mountains. Your child paints a 3-layer study: light blue far, medium middle, dark near.

questions.q: What is atmospheric perspective?
questions.a: Making distant objects lighter, bluer/grayer and less detailed to show depth, as the air does.

days.guide: Compare Bierstadt's Yosemite with a photo. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How did Bierstadt exaggerate Yosemite?
questions.a: He made cliffs taller and more dramatic, and the golden glowing light more intense than in reality, to create a sense of awe (the sublime).

days.guide: Compare to a Native American design or modern landscape; discuss different criteria for judging each.

questions.q: Why might you judge a Navajo weaving differently from a Hudson River School painting?
questions.a: They have different purposes and traditions—one uses symbolic geometric patterns, the other aims at realistic, dramatic scenery.

days.guide: Write a paragraph interpreting the mood of one landscape with evidence. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Which evidence supports a mood interpretation?
questions.a: Specific colors, light, weather, composition and details in the painting.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = states the mood and supports it with at least three specific details (color, light, composition); 3 = two details; 2 = one; 1 = no evidence. Atmospheric perspective study: three layers clearly lighter/bluer with distance.

weeks.prep: Gather watercolor paper, watercolors, brushes (one large flat, one round), masking tape, salt, and a reference photo or outdoor view. Tape paper edges to the board.
misconceptions: Painting dark colors first in watercolor. Work light to dark; you can't easily lighten watercolor.
Overworking wet paint. Let layers dry before adding detail.

days.guide: On a sampler: flat wash, wet-on-wet (paint on wet paper), dry brush (little water on brush), and salt on wet paint for texture.

questions.q: What happens when you sprinkle salt on wet watercolor?
questions.a: The salt absorbs pigment and water, creating a speckled starburst texture.

days.guide: Sketch the landscape lightly with foreground, middle ground and background. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Which ground is closest to the viewer?
questions.a: The foreground.

days.guide: Paint the sky and distant layers with light, cool washes. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why use cool, light colors for the background?
questions.a: Atmospheric perspective makes distant things appear lighter and bluer.

days.guide: Paint the middle ground and foreground with warmer, darker colors and detail. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Where should the most detail go?
questions.a: In the foreground, closest to the viewer.

days.guide: Your child checks: light-to-dark layering, three grounds, atmospheric perspective; notes one area to refine.

questions.q: What would you refine?
questions.a: Answer varies; e.g., 'darken the foreground trees for more contrast.'

weeks.assessment_key: Technique sampler: four techniques labeled and visible. Progress check: three grounds, background light and cool, foreground darker/warmer with more detail. Proficient = all present.

weeks.prep: Have the landscape painting, fine brushes, black construction paper slightly larger than the painting, a ruler, and a glue stick. Print the four critique steps: Describe (what do you see?), Analyze (how are elements and principles used?), Interpret (what mood or meaning?), Judge (is it successful and why?).
misconceptions: Thinking critique means criticism. A critique is a careful look at what works and what could be stronger, supported by evidence.
Jumping straight to 'I like it / I don't.' Describe and analyze first so the judgment is backed by evidence.

days.guide: Your child adds final details with a fine brush and darkens foreground values or lightens distant ones to strengthen depth.

questions.q: Name two ways to make the landscape look deeper.
questions.a: Darken and add detail to the foreground; keep the background lighter, cooler and less detailed; overlap shapes.

days.guide: Your child leads family through the four critique steps, asking each question aloud and listening to answers.

questions.q: What happens in the 'interpret' step?
questions.a: You explain the mood or meaning of the artwork, supported by what you saw (e.g., 'The cool blues and soft light feel peaceful').

days.guide: Your child chooses one suggestion from the critique and revises (e.g., adds shadows, strengthens a focal point).

questions.q: Why is revision part of the art process?
questions.a: Artists improve work by responding to feedback and fresh eyes.

days.guide: Center the painting on the black paper with even borders (measure all four sides) and glue neatly.

questions.q: Why do you measure the borders of a mat?
questions.a: Even borders look neat and professional and keep the focus on the artwork.

days.guide: Your child writes an artist statement (subject, techniques, mood, revision) and files the painting.

questions.q: Which watercolor techniques did you use, and where?
questions.a: Answer varies; e.g., 'wet-on-wet in the sky, dry brush for grass texture, salt on the rocks.'

weeks.assessment_key: Landscape rubric (1–4 each): depth through foreground/middle/background; atmospheric perspective; at least two watercolor techniques used purposefully; craftsmanship (clean edges, neat mat). Artist statement proficient if it names techniques, describes mood with evidence, and explains the revision made after critique.

weeks.prep: Find Smithsonian Folkways recordings (free excerpts at folkways.si.edu): a Native American song (e.g., a Lakota, Navajo or Ojibwe song) and a 'lining out' psalm (often found by searching 'lined-out hymn'). Gather materials for a drum or rattle: an oatmeal canister or coffee can with a balloon or packing tape top; a bottle or container with dried beans.
misconceptions: Thinking all Native American music sounds the same. There are hundreds of nations with distinct languages, songs and instruments.
Thinking vocables are 'nonsense.' Vocables are syllables without dictionary meaning but are an important, intentional part of many songs.

days.guide: Listen to the recording; your child describes the instruments (drum, rattle, flute), the steady drumbeat, and vocables (syllables like 'hey-ya').

questions.q: What are vocables?
questions.a: Sung syllables that don't have a word meaning but are a meaningful part of the song.

days.guide: Chart purposes of music (ceremony, storytelling, celebration, work, lullaby) with examples.

questions.q: Name three purposes of music in a culture.
questions.a: Ceremony/worship, storytelling, celebration, work, healing, lullabies.

days.guide: Listen to a lined-out psalm: a leader sings a line and the congregation repeats. Try call-and-response with your child.

questions.q: Why did colonial congregations use 'lining out'?
questions.a: Many people didn't have hymn books or couldn't read music, so a leader sang each line and everyone repeated it.

days.guide: Make a drum or rattle and play a steady-beat pattern. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How does a drum make sound?
questions.a: The surface vibrates when struck, making the air vibrate.

days.guide: Your child writes how music connected to daily life in one culture, citing a recording. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Give an example of a connection between music and daily life.
questions.a: Example: colonial psalm singing was part of weekly worship; a Native American song might accompany a ceremony or dance.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening log: for each recording, the culture, instruments, purpose and musical features (steady beat, vocables, call and response). Written response rubric: 4 = explains a connection to daily life and cites a specific recording and detail; 3 = connection without specific evidence; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Print the lyrics for 'Yankee Doodle,' 'The Star-Spangled Banner,' 'America the Beautiful,' and 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee.' Find a recording of each. Recorder music for 'Yankee Doodle' (G G A B G B A, in G).
misconceptions: Thinking 'Yankee Doodle' was always a patriotic song. British soldiers sang it to mock colonists; Patriots adopted it with pride.
Thinking 'The Star-Spangled Banner' was written during the Revolution. It was written during the War of 1812 (1814).

days.guide: Read the history; play 'Yankee Doodle' on recorder. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How did 'Yankee Doodle' change meaning?
questions.a: British soldiers sang it to make fun of colonists, but Patriots made it their own proud song.

days.guide: Read about Francis Scott Key watching the bombardment of Fort McHenry (Baltimore, 1814); sing the first verse, noting the wide range.

questions.q: What event inspired 'The Star-Spangled Banner'?
questions.a: The British bombardment of Fort McHenry in 1814 during the War of 1812; Key saw the flag still flying at dawn.

days.guide: Learn 'America the Beautiful' (Katharine Lee Bates, inspired by the view from Pikes Peak); list geographic images.

questions.q: List three geographic images in 'America the Beautiful.'
questions.a: Spacious skies, amber waves of grain, purple mountain majesties, the fruited plain, from sea to shining sea.

days.guide: Choose dynamics and tempo to express one song's meaning; record it. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why might you sing the end of 'America the Beautiful' louder?
questions.a: To build to a proud, powerful ending expressing the song's ideal.

days.guide: Perform two songs and explain each song's ideal. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What ideal does 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee' express?
questions.a: Liberty/freedom ('sweet land of liberty').

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric: 4 = accurate melody and lyrics, chosen dynamics/tempo match meaning, confident; 3 = minor errors; 2 = many errors; 1 = incomplete. Explanation: Star-Spangled Banner — courage, survival of the nation; America the Beautiful — beauty and unity; My Country 'Tis of Thee — liberty; Yankee Doodle — Patriot pride.

weeks.prep: Find recordings of 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' (e.g., the Fisk Jubilee Singers' historic version), 'Wade in the Water,' and 'Follow the Drinking Gourd,' plus two different performances of one spiritual. Print lyrics. Read a short background on spirituals (Library of Congress). Note: historians debate how often songs were used as literal codes, so present code meanings as 'possible' or 'traditionally told.'
misconceptions: Thinking spirituals were just sad songs. They expressed sorrow but also hope, faith, freedom and resistance.
Treating 'code song' stories as proven fact. Some meanings are traditional interpretations that historians still debate.

days.guide: Listen to 'Swing Low'; explain spirituals were created by enslaved African Americans, blending African musical traditions (call-and-response, syncopation) with Christian hymns.

questions.q: Who created spirituals, and what did they express?
questions.a: Enslaved African Americans; they expressed faith, suffering, hope and longing for freedom.

days.guide: Read lyrics of 'Follow the Drinking Gourd' and 'Wade in the Water'; discuss possible hidden meanings.

questions.q: What is the 'drinking gourd' traditionally said to mean?
questions.a: The Big Dipper, which points to the North Star — a guide north toward freedom.

days.guide: Learn a call-and-response work song (e.g., 'Pick a Bale of Cotton' or a sea shanty); discuss rhythm.

questions.q: How did rhythm help people work together?
questions.a: A steady beat let workers move in time, coordinate tasks and make hard work feel lighter.

days.guide: Compare two performances of the same spiritual for tempo, dynamics and timbre. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is timbre?
questions.a: The unique tone color of a voice or instrument.

days.guide: Your child sings a spiritual with chosen expressive qualities and writes about performers' intent.

questions.q: Why might a performer sing a spiritual slowly and softly?
questions.a: To express sorrow, reverence or longing.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening comparison: compares tempo, dynamics, timbre and accompaniment of two performances with specific examples (4 = all four, 3 = three, 2 = two, 1 = one). Performance: expressive choices that match the song's meaning, accurate pitch and lyrics.

weeks.prep: Print lyrics for 'Low Bridge, Everybody Down (Erie Canal),' 'Shenandoah,' 'Oh! Susanna' and 'Sweet Betsy from Pike'; find recordings. Recorder or virtual keyboard for 'Oh! Susanna.'
misconceptions: Confusing verse and chorus. The chorus (refrain) repeats the same words; verses have new words each time.
Thinking folk songs have one 'correct' version. Folk songs were passed down orally and changed over time.

days.guide: Learn 'Erie Canal'; your child marks verse and chorus. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What does 'Low bridge, everybody down' warn about?
questions.a: Low bridges over the canal—people on the boat had to duck.

days.guide: Sing 'Shenandoah'; discuss how long phrases create longing. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How does the melody of 'Shenandoah' create a feeling of longing?
questions.a: Long, slow, flowing phrases and wide leaps make it sound wistful and yearning.

days.guide: Learn Stephen Foster's 'Oh! Susanna' (1848); play its melody. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why did 'Oh! Susanna' become popular with the Forty-Niners?
questions.a: Gold Rush travelers sang it on their way to California.

days.guide: Add a body-percussion or drum accompaniment. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is accompaniment?
questions.a: Music that supports the melody (like a drum or chords).

days.guide: Lead a family sing-along of 3 songs; write a reflection. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What can folk songs teach about history?
questions.a: They show daily life, work, travel and feelings of people in the past (e.g., canal workers, pioneers).

weeks.assessment_key: Sing-along rubric: 4 = leads 3 songs confidently with accurate lyrics and an accompaniment; 3 = minor errors; 2 = needs much support; 1 = incomplete. Reflection proficient if it links at least two songs to historical events or daily life (e.g., Erie Canal transportation, Gold Rush).

weeks.prep: Open images from the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian: Pueblo pottery (e.g., Maria Martinez's black-on-black ware), Navajo (Diné) weavings, Haudenosaunee raised beadwork. Read the museum labels. Gather graph paper, colored pencils, and two colors of construction paper cut into strips for weaving.
misconceptions: Copying sacred symbols. Some designs have spiritual meanings and belong to specific nations; create your own symbols instead.
Thinking Native American art is only historical. Native artists continue these traditions and create new art today.

days.guide: Your child describes patterns in each art form (geometric, symmetry, repetition, color). Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What kind of symmetry is common in Navajo weavings?
questions.a: Bilateral (mirror) symmetry with geometric shapes like diamonds and zigzags.

days.guide: Read museum labels; discuss why some symbols are sacred. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why shouldn't you copy sacred symbols?
questions.a: They have spiritual or cultural meaning to a specific people; copying them can be disrespectful.

days.guide: Design a symmetrical geometric pattern on graph paper using personal symbols. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is a motif?
questions.a: A repeated design element or symbol in a pattern.

days.guide: Weave a paper mat with over-under pattern. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What is the over-under structure?
questions.a: Strips alternate going over and under, creating a strong woven pattern.

days.guide: Write how art preserves culture and explain personal symbols. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: How does art preserve culture?
questions.a: It passes on stories, beliefs, skills and identity from generation to generation.

weeks.assessment_key: Pattern design: symmetrical, repeated motifs, personal (not copied sacred) symbols, neat craftsmanship. Reflection rubric: 4 = explains how art preserves culture with an example and meaning of own symbols; 3 = one missing; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Find John Singleton Copley's 'Paul Revere' (1768, Museum of Fine Arts Boston) and an Ammi Phillips folk portrait (e.g., 'Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog'). Set up a mirror, pencils and paper. Facial proportions: eyes halfway down the head; nose bottom halfway between eyes and chin; mouth one-third of the way from nose to chin; ears between eye and nose lines.
misconceptions: Drawing eyes near the top of the head. Eyes are about halfway down the head.
Thinking folk art is 'bad' art. It follows different goals (bold patterns, flat shapes) and is judged by different criteria.

days.guide: Analyze Copley's portrait; list clues about Revere's job and status. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What clues show Paul Revere's job?
questions.a: He holds a silver teapot and engraving tools lie on the table—he was a silversmith; he's in work clothes (shirtsleeves, vest).

days.guide: Compare professional and folk portraits; discuss different criteria. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How does Ammi Phillips's style differ from Copley's?
questions.a: Phillips used flatter shapes, bold colors and simplified forms; Copley used realistic detail, light and shadow.

days.guide: Teach facial proportions; draw a self-portrait from a mirror. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Where are the eyes on a face?
questions.a: About halfway between the top of the head and the chin.

days.guide: Add symbolic objects showing interests. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why did colonial portraitists include objects?
questions.a: To show the sitter's job, status, interests or values.

days.guide: Compare interpretation of Copley's portrait with a family member's; write about differences.

questions.q: Why might two people interpret the same portrait differently?
questions.a: They notice different details and bring different experiences and knowledge.

weeks.assessment_key: Self-portrait rubric: 4 = accurate proportions (eyes halfway, nose, mouth, ears placed correctly), value shading, 2+ symbolic objects explained; 3 = minor errors; 2 = proportions off or no symbols; 1 = incomplete. Comparison: proficient if it explains specific differences and reasons.

weeks.prep: Find Paul Revere's engraving 'The Bloody Massacre' (1770) and Benjamin Franklin's 'Join, or Die' (1754). Gather foam trays or craft foam, dull pencil, washable ink or tempera, a brayer or roller, and paper. Cover the table.
misconceptions: Forgetting the print reverses. Letters and words must be carved backward.
Carving too shallow. Lines must be pressed deeply so ink doesn't fill them.

days.guide: Study the two prints; explain how prints spread messages. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How was Revere's Boston Massacre engraving propaganda?
questions.a: It showed British soldiers firing in an orderly line at peaceful colonists, exaggerating events to stir anger against Britain.

days.guide: Design an image with a message, remembering it reverses. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: If you want 'HELP' to read correctly in the print, how must you carve it?
questions.a: Backward (mirror image).

days.guide: Press the design into foam with a dull pencil, checking depth. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why must lines be deep?
questions.a: So ink stays on the raised surface and the lines print white.

days.guide: Roll ink, pull an edition of 4 prints, number and sign them (1/4, 2/4...). Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What does '2/4' written on a print mean?
questions.a: The second print in an edition of four.

days.guide: Choose the best print and explain its message and tool care. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What did 'Join, or Die' mean?
questions.a: The colonies (snake pieces) had to unite or be destroyed.

weeks.assessment_key: Print edition: 4 consistent prints, numbered and signed, clear image with reversed text correct. Explanation: message clearly stated; tool care (clean brayer, wipe ink). Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Find images of Harriet Powers's Bible Quilt (1886, Smithsonian) and a Gee's Bend quilt. Gather colored paper, glue, ruler, graph paper, and invite family members to each make a square.
misconceptions: Thinking quilts are only for warmth. Many quilts tell stories, preserve history and are considered fine art.
Thinking unity means everything is the same. Unity is a sense of belonging together; variety adds interest.

days.guide: Study Powers's quilt and a Gee's Bend quilt; discuss storytelling. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: How did Harriet Powers tell stories in her quilt?
questions.a: Appliquéd panels showing Bible stories with figures and symbols.

days.guide: Draw Log Cabin, Flying Geese and Star blocks. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What shape is common in Flying Geese?
questions.a: Triangles (a large triangle with two smaller ones).

days.guide: Design an original quilt square telling about your family. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What principle of design is shown by repeating shapes?
questions.a: Repetition (pattern), which creates rhythm and unity.

days.guide: Join family squares into a paper quilt. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: How does the quilt show unity and variety?
questions.a: Common colors or borders unify; different designs add variety.

days.guide: Present the square and answer questions on early American art and messages. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Name two early American artworks that carried messages.
questions.a: Revere's Boston Massacre engraving, 'Join, or Die,' Harriet Powers's quilt.

weeks.assessment_key: Quilt square rubric: 4 = original design, clear family story, neat craftsmanship, uses repetition/symmetry; 3 = minor issues; 2 = unclear story; 1 = incomplete. Unit reflection: explains how prints, portraits and quilts carried messages with examples.

weeks.prep: Bookmark musictheory.net note-identification exercise (treble clef). Print 'Ode to Joy' and 'Twinkle, Twinkle' notation and an 8-measure recorder melody. Recorder low D = thumb + all three left fingers + three right fingers (only the pinky hole open); check your fingering chart for F-sharp, which differs slightly between baroque and German recorders.
misconceptions: Thinking a skip means skipping a line on the staff. A skip moves from a line to the next line (or space to next space), skipping one note name.
Mixing up lines and spaces. Treble lines (bottom to top) are E G B D F; spaces are F A C E.

days.guide: Play 4 melodies; your child draws their contour (up, down, wavy). Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What is melodic contour?
questions.a: The shape of a melody as it moves up and down.

days.guide: Identify steps (next note), skips (skip one note) and leaps (bigger) in 'Ode to Joy' and 'Twinkle.'

questions.q: In 'Twinkle, Twinkle,' the notes go C C G G. Is C to G a step, skip or leap?
questions.a: A leap (a fifth).

days.guide: Your child practices on musictheory.net until scoring 90%. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Name the lines of the treble staff from bottom to top.
questions.a: E, G, B, D, F.

days.guide: Teach low D and F-sharp; play a warm-up D-E-F#-G-A and back. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why does low D need gentle breath?
questions.a: Low notes squeak if you blow too hard.

days.guide: Take the note-naming and interval quiz; play an 8-measure melody. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Name the spaces of the treble staff from bottom to top.
questions.a: F, A, C, E.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: name 10 notes on the treble staff (lines E G B D F, spaces F A C E) and label 5 intervals as step, skip or leap. Proficient = 90% on notes, 4/5 intervals. Melody performance: correct notes and steady rhythm (4 = no errors; 3 = 1–2; 2 = several; 1 = incomplete).

weeks.prep: Open Chrome Music Lab (Piano Roll or Chords) or a virtual keyboard. Choose 6 excerpts (3 major, e.g., 'Happy Birthday'; 3 minor, e.g., 'Greensleeves,' Grieg's 'In the Hall of the Mountain King'). Major scale pattern: W W H W W W H.
misconceptions: Thinking minor always means sad. Minor often sounds darker or mysterious but can be energetic.
Thinking a half step skips a key. A half step is the very next key (black or white); a whole step skips one key.

days.guide: Play 6 excerpts; your child identifies major or minor and describes mood. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What mood do minor keys often create?
questions.a: Darker, sad, mysterious or serious.

days.guide: Build C major using W W H W W W H on a keyboard. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Where are the half steps in C major?
questions.a: Between E–F and B–C.

days.guide: Play G major on recorder: G A B C D E F# G. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: Which note is sharp in G major?
questions.a: F-sharp.

days.guide: Play 'Hot Cross Buns' in major (E D C), then minor (E-flat D C); compare. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: What change turned 'Hot Cross Buns' from major to minor?
questions.a: Lowering the third note of the scale (E to E-flat).

days.guide: Listening quiz; perform the G major scale. Give it without notes, then review each missed item together using the answer key below and have your child correct it in their own words.

questions.q: What is the tonic?
questions.a: The first and home note of a scale.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening quiz: 6 excerpts correctly labeled major/minor (proficient 5/6). Scale performance: correct notes including F#, even rhythm. Scale pattern: W W H W W W H.

weeks.prep: Print lyrics for 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat,' 'Frère Jacques,' 'This Old Man,' 'Skip to My Lou,' and 'Clementine.' Open Chrome Music Lab Chords. C major I chord = C-E-G; V chord = G-B-D.
misconceptions: Thinking harmony means singing the same notes. Harmony is two or more different pitches sounding together.
Losing your part in a round. Cover one ear and focus on your own melody.

days.guide: Sing rounds; voice 2 enters when voice 1 reaches the second phrase. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: When does the second voice enter in 'Row, Row, Row Your Boat'?
questions.a: When the first voice begins 'Gently down the stream.'

days.guide: Sing two partner songs at the same time. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is a partner song?
questions.a: Two different songs that fit together harmonically when sung at the same time.

days.guide: Build I and V in C; listen for changes in a song. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What notes make the I chord in C major?
questions.a: C, E, G.

days.guide: Accompany 'Clementine' with I and V on keyboard or ukulele. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What notes make the V chord in C?
questions.a: G, B, D.

days.guide: Write I or V above lyrics; perform. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why does a song often end on the I chord?
questions.a: It sounds finished and resolved—home.

weeks.assessment_key: Round performance: holds own part through the round (4 = no errors; 3 = minor; 2 = loses part; 1 = cannot). Chord analysis: I and V marked correctly above lyrics at chord changes (proficient = 80%).

weeks.prep: Find recordings: Mozart's 'Twelve Variations on Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,' K. 265; Beethoven's 'Für Elise'; Mouret's 'Rondeau.' Prepare colored shapes (A = red circle, B = blue square, C = green triangle).
misconceptions: Thinking a section must be identical to repeat. A returning section may change slightly but is recognizable.
Confusing rondo and ABA. Rondo has A returning between several different sections (ABACA).

days.guide: Listen to two short pieces; label A and B with shapes. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is ternary (ABA) form?
questions.a: A section, contrasting B section, then A returns.

days.guide: Map Mouret's 'Rondeau' (ABACA). Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: In a rondo, which section keeps returning?
questions.a: The A section.

days.guide: Listen to Mozart's variations; describe how 3 change the theme. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How can a composer vary a theme?
questions.a: Change rhythm, add notes, change from major to minor, change tempo or dynamics.

days.guide: Create a movement routine changing with each section of 'Für Elise' (A–B–A–C–A). Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What form is 'Für Elise'?
questions.a: Rondo (A B A C A).

days.guide: Listening assessment: form, major/minor, contour. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is theme and variations?
questions.a: A melody presented and then changed in several ways.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening map: correctly shows sections for 'Rondeau' (ABACA). Unit 6 assessment: identifies form (AB, ABA, rondo, theme & variations), major vs minor, and contour of 3 melodies. Proficient = 80%.

weeks.prep: Gather cardstock, scissors, glue, tape. Find images of Alexander Calder's mobiles and stabiles and Ruth Asawa's looped wire sculptures (de Young Museum, San Francisco).
misconceptions: Thinking sculpture is only about the material. Empty space (negative space) is part of the design.
Building flat. A freestanding sculpture must look interesting from all sides.

days.guide: Practice curling, folding, scoring, fringing and tab joints. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Why score paper before folding?
questions.a: A light crease line makes a crisp, straight fold.

days.guide: Look at Calder and Asawa; discuss positive and negative space. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: What is negative space in a sculpture?
questions.a: The empty space around and through the sculpture.

days.guide: Build a freestanding abstract sculpture at least 8 inches tall. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: How can you make a tall paper sculpture stable?
questions.a: A wide base, folded or rolled columns, and tab joints.

days.guide: Photograph from 4 angles; fix weak sides. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why view a sculpture from all sides?
questions.a: It's three-dimensional and seen from every angle.

days.guide: Write about positive and negative space. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Give an example of positive space in your sculpture.
questions.a: The paper forms themselves.

weeks.assessment_key: Sculpture rubric: 4 = freestanding, 8+ inches, uses 3+ paper techniques, interesting from all sides, intentional negative space; 3 = minor issues; 2 = unstable or flat; 1 = incomplete. Reflection explains positive/negative space with examples.

weeks.prep: Gather air-dry clay (or salt dough: 2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, about ¾ cup water, kneaded smooth), a plastic knife, fork or toothpick for scoring, a water cup, a placemat, and plastic wrap or a zip bag. Make a little 'slip' by mixing clay with water to a yogurt-like paste.
misconceptions: Joining pieces by just pressing them together. Without scoring and slip, pieces crack apart as they dry.
Making walls very uneven. Thin spots crack and thick spots dry slowly; aim for walls about as thick as a pencil.

days.guide: Demonstrate: roll a ball, press your thumb into the center, then pinch while turning the ball a little each time. Your child makes a pinch pot and checks wall thickness by feel.

questions.q: How do you keep pinch-pot walls even?
questions.a: Pinch with the same pressure while rotating the pot a little after each pinch, working from the bottom up.

days.guide: Roll a coil (even 'snake') and a slab (flattened with a rolling pin). Join two pieces: scratch both surfaces, add slip, press and smooth the seam.

questions.q: What are the steps of score and slip?
questions.a: Scratch (score) both surfaces, add slip (wet clay paste), press together, and smooth the seam.

days.guide: Your child sketches an animal vessel or expressive figure that combines ideas from two inspirations (e.g., a pinch-pot owl inspired by Pueblo pottery and a pet), labeling which method builds each part.

questions.q: Which method would you use for a tall, round vessel?
questions.a: Stacked coils (or a pinch pot base with coils added on).

days.guide: Your child builds the main form, joining every attachment with score and slip. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why should solid parts be no thicker than about an inch?
questions.a: Thick parts dry slowly and may crack; thinner, even parts dry evenly.

days.guide: Add texture with a fork, toothpick or pressed objects; wrap tightly in plastic and write next steps.

questions.q: Why wrap the unfinished sculpture in plastic?
questions.a: To keep it from drying out so you can keep working on it next time.

weeks.assessment_key: Technique test pieces: 4 = pinch pot with even walls, smooth coil, flat slab, and a joint that holds when gently tugged; 3 = one weakness; 2 = joints fail or walls very uneven; 1 = incomplete. Sculpture plan: sketch shows two inspirations and labels building methods.

weeks.prep: Make sure the sculpture is completely dry (air-dry clay usually takes 24–72 hours). Gather fine sandpaper or a damp sponge, acrylic or tempera paint, brushes, clear glue or Mod Podge, and newspaper.
misconceptions: Painting before the sculpture is fully dry. Paint can crack or the piece can mold; check it's dry and room temperature.
Skipping cleanup. Craftsmanship includes caring for tools and workspace.

days.guide: Smooth rough edges gently with sandpaper or a damp sponge, supporting thin parts. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why support thin parts while sanding?
questions.a: Dry clay is fragile and can break.

days.guide: Paint with a planned color scheme, base colors first, then details. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Name a color scheme you could use.
questions.a: Complementary, analogous or monochromatic.

days.guide: Seal with Mod Podge or clear glue; clean brushes and workspace. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: Why seal a painted sculpture?
questions.a: To protect the paint and give a finished look.

days.guide: Write a display plan (pedestal, label, lighting). Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why does lighting matter in display?
questions.a: It shows form and texture with highlights and shadows.

days.guide: Present the sculpture and explain revisions. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: What is craftsmanship?
questions.a: Care and skill in making the artwork—smooth surfaces, neat painting, secure joins.

weeks.assessment_key: Craftsmanship rubric (1–4 each): secure joins, smooth surfaces, neat painting with planned color scheme, sealed finish. Display plan proficient if it names pedestal/surface, label content and lighting with reasons.

weeks.prep: Find images of Andy Goldsworthy's nature art (leaves, stones, ice) and Louise Nevelson's wooden assemblages. Gather recycled objects (caps, cardboard tubes, buttons), a shoebox lid painted one color, glue, and a camera. Choose a safe outdoor spot for environmental art.
misconceptions: Thinking art has to last forever. Ephemeral art is meant to change or disappear; the photograph records it.
Gluing random objects. Assemblage works when objects are arranged by color, shape and repetition into a unified design.

days.guide: Compare Goldsworthy and Nevelson: materials and meaning. Go through it once together, then a second time while your child notes what they observe; prompt with 'What do you notice? What makes you say that?'

questions.q: Why did Louise Nevelson paint assemblages one color?
questions.a: To unify many different found objects so viewers focus on shape, pattern and shadow.

days.guide: Collect materials and sort by color, shape and texture. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Why sort materials before building?
questions.a: It helps you see patterns and plan unity.

days.guide: Build an outdoor ephemeral sculpture; photograph it. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: What does ephemeral mean?
questions.a: Lasting only a short time.

days.guide: Assemble a found-object sculpture in a painted shoebox lid. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What is an assemblage?
questions.a: A 3D artwork made by combining found objects.

days.guide: Write a comparison of the two sculptures; add photos to the portfolio. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How are your two sculptures different?
questions.a: One is temporary and natural; the other is permanent and made of found objects.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 portfolio entry: photos of both sculptures with a written comparison (materials, permanence, design principles, meaning). Rubric: 4 = clear comparison with art terms (unity, repetition, positive/negative space); 3 = some terms; 2 = vague; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Find Britten's 'The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra' (1946, based on a theme by Henry Purcell) and the Classics for Kids instrument game. Print 16 instrument pictures. Gather supplies for a homemade instrument (shoebox and rubber bands; straws; glass bottles and water).
misconceptions: Thinking the saxophone is brass. It's metal but a woodwind (uses a reed).
Thinking the piano is only a string instrument. It has strings but they're struck by hammers; it's often grouped with percussion or keyboards.

days.guide: Teach the four families: strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion; sort 16 pictures. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Which family does the flute belong to?
questions.a: Woodwinds.

days.guide: Listen to Britten; list instruments as featured. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: In what order does Britten present the families?
questions.a: Woodwinds, strings, brass, percussion (then a fugue with all).

days.guide: Play the instrument game; describe timbres with adjectives. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: Describe the timbre of a trumpet.
questions.a: Bright, brassy, bold.

days.guide: Build a homemade instrument; explain how it makes sound. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How does a rubber-band guitar make sound?
questions.a: The bands vibrate; tighter or thinner bands vibrate faster and make higher pitches.

days.guide: Listening quiz identifying 8 instruments. Have your child work independently; afterward, go over any errors together and let them explain the correct answer back to you.

questions.q: Which family makes sound by buzzing lips?
questions.a: Brass.

weeks.assessment_key: Listening quiz: identifies 8 instruments (e.g., violin, cello, flute, clarinet, trumpet, trombone, timpani, snare drum) and their families. Proficient = 6/8.

weeks.prep: Find Prokofiev's 'Peter and the Wolf' (1936) and Grieg's 'In the Hall of the Mountain King' (from Peer Gynt). Gather household sound makers. Choose a short story from ELA.
misconceptions: Thinking program music needs words. It tells stories with instruments, themes, tempo and dynamics.
Thinking louder means faster. Tempo (speed) and dynamics (volume) are separate.

days.guide: Listen and match characters to instruments. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Which instrument plays Peter? The wolf?
questions.a: Peter = strings; wolf = French horns (bird = flute, duck = oboe, cat = clarinet, grandfather = bassoon).

days.guide: Graph tempo and dynamics building in 'Mountain King.' Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What happens to tempo and dynamics in 'In the Hall of the Mountain King'?
questions.a: Both gradually increase—accelerando and crescendo—building to a wild ending.

days.guide: Plan a sound story assigning sounds to characters/events. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: What is a leitmotif?
questions.a: A short musical theme representing a character or idea.

days.guide: Improvise and record the sound story. Start with a slow demonstration, then have your child repeat it several times while you give one piece of specific feedback at a time and praise effort.

questions.q: How could you show a chase in sound?
questions.a: Faster tempo and louder dynamics.

days.guide: Play for family; explain choices. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What is a crescendo?
questions.a: Gradually getting louder.

weeks.assessment_key: Sound story rubric: 4 = each character has a distinct sound/motif, tempo and dynamics change with events, clear explanation; 3 = most; 2 = few; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Open Chrome Music Lab Song Maker (set to 4 bars, C major) and find the opening of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony. Print staff paper and a criteria checklist: memorable motif, question and answer phrases, ends on the tonic (C), repetition with variation, steady rhythm, accompaniment.
misconceptions: Thinking a composition needs many different ideas. Strong melodies repeat and develop a few motifs.
Ending on a random note. An 'answer' phrase sounds finished when it ends on the tonic (home note).

days.guide: Listen to Beethoven's Fifth opening (short-short-short-long); show how the motif repeats at different pitches. Your child invents 3 motifs of 3–5 notes.

questions.q: What is a motif?
questions.a: A short musical idea that is repeated and developed through a piece.

days.guide: Compose a 4-measure 'question' phrase ending on a note other than C, and a 4-measure 'answer' ending on C.

questions.q: Why does the answer phrase end on the tonic?
questions.a: The tonic sounds like 'home,' so the music feels finished (a cadence).

days.guide: Add a percussion pattern and I–V accompaniment (C and G chords) in Song Maker. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What two chords make a simple accompaniment in C major?
questions.a: C major (I) and G major (V).

days.guide: Write the melody on staff paper or save the Song Maker link and screenshot. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why write the music down?
questions.a: So it can be performed again by you or others exactly as composed.

days.guide: Share the draft; family uses the criteria checklist. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Give one criterion of a strong melody.
questions.a: A memorable motif, repetition, ending on the tonic, or a clear phrase structure.

weeks.assessment_key: Composition draft: 8 measures (question + answer), motif repeated or varied, ends on tonic C, percussion and I–V accompaniment, notation or saved link. Proficient = 5 of 6 criteria.

weeks.prep: Have the composition, feedback checklist, recorder or keyboard. Teach expressive marks: tempo words (Largo = slow, Andante = walking, Allegro = fast) and dynamics (p = soft, mf = medium loud, f = loud, crescendo/decrescendo).
misconceptions: Thinking revision means starting over. Revision improves specific parts based on feedback.
Leaving out tempo and dynamics. They tell performers how the music should feel.

days.guide: Revise based on feedback; document changes (before/after). Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why document changes?
questions.a: To show growth and explain choices.

days.guide: Add tempo and dynamics to the notation. Show a quick example, watch your child's first few minutes of work, then step back and check in with one specific suggestion.

questions.q: What does 'p' mean? 'f'?
questions.a: p = piano (soft); f = forte (loud).

days.guide: Practice performing on recorder/keyboard or prepare the digital version. Model it once yourself (or show a short video), let your child try, and give one specific cue-based correction before the next attempt; finish with a full run-through.

questions.q: What tempo marking means 'fast'?
questions.a: Allegro.

days.guide: Write a program note: title, mood, choices. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What is a program note?
questions.a: A short written explanation for the audience about a piece.

days.guide: Present with the program note; evaluate with criteria. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: How do your dynamics support the mood?
questions.a: Answer varies; should connect markings to mood (e.g., soft for calm).

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric (1–4 each): revised melody with documented changes; tempo and dynamics marked; performance or polished digital version; program note explains title, mood and choices. Proficient = 3+ each.

weeks.prep: Gather the year's artwork, index cards, and access to Google Arts & Culture for a virtual museum tour.
misconceptions: Thinking a portfolio is all your work. A curated portfolio selects pieces that show growth and variety.
Choosing only favorites. Include pieces showing progress, even early ones.

days.guide: Take a virtual tour; list curator responsibilities (choose works, arrange, write labels, care for art).

questions.q: What does a curator do?
questions.a: Selects, organizes and presents artworks for an exhibition and cares for them.

days.guide: Select 6 pieces showing growth and variety. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: Why include an early piece?
questions.a: It shows how your skills grew over the year.

days.guide: Write a reflection for each: learned and would change. Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: What should a reflection include?
questions.a: What you learned, techniques used, and what you'd change.

days.guide: Choose an exhibition title and theme; order the artworks. Talk through ideas aloud first, then have your child write; check that the work uses this week's vocabulary and specific examples rather than general statements.

questions.q: How can the order of artworks tell a story?
questions.a: Arranging by time, theme or technique leads viewers through growth or an idea.

days.guide: Present the plan to a parent. Pause often to have your child explain what they see, hear or read in their own words, and write down two or three key points together.

questions.q: Why does an exhibition need a theme?
questions.a: It connects the works and helps viewers understand the show.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio selection: 6 pieces showing variety (drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture) and growth. Reflections: 4 = each piece has specific learning and revision ideas with art terms; 3 = most; 2 = brief; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Gather mats or construction paper, painter's tape, label cards, and a wall or tables with good light.
misconceptions: Hanging art at random heights. Hang centers at about eye level and space evenly.
Writing long labels. Museum labels are short: title, artist, medium, date, and one or two sentences.

days.guide: Mount or mat each 2D artwork neatly. Demonstrate the first step briefly, then let your child work independently; coach with one specific tip at a time rather than fixing the work for them.

questions.q: Why mat artwork?
questions.a: It frames and protects the piece and looks professional.

days.guide: Write museum labels (title, medium, date, description). Let your child draft independently, then read it together and ask for one more specific detail or example wherever the answer is vague.

questions.q: Write a sample museum label.
